translations.3b49d1f2f06e3c601fe41c22: N2 to N3: 4 weeks approving without correcting—only for the no-risk part.
translations.2838f38f8c82ccc6de458e7c: N3 to N4: 2 months of clean reports and alarms working.
translations.8ece2c031389f8b31682c8d4: When in doubt, go down: the lowest level is always the safe answer.
translations.0ed1dc32179da2872fcfa805: ⟪P0⟫6⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫Calculate the level for 3 cases from the gallery⟪P3⟫
translations.2077756fd25fade7942ffa0b: Now you apply the whole rule to three ready-made Agent Sheet cases from the gallery: the real estate company's lead triager, the restaurant's inventory controller, and the agency's campaign reporter. For each one, write down the action, the risks, and whether there is an official source, then calculate the level before opening the link. After that, compare with what the Agent Sheet calculated. The full gallery is at ⟪P0⟫
translations.e931027151e3ffec2f79c2cc: Reading the rule is easy; applying it to real cases is what locks in the reasoning. The three cases were chosen because they represent three different levels: one stuck because of risk, one open because it's internal, and one that touches an entire process. If you get all three right, you can calculate the level of any task in your business.
translations.b58dfa427cd289a8a5df6a17: Real estate: executes, with money and people from outside.
translations.cf6cc0a3368d82c83168e6b8: Restaurant: executes, internal, reversible, with a source.
translations.5f5ff339b1a3139cad327c38: Agency: coordinates an internal process, with a source.
translations.8ce6ae1debaa53db5ab96456: Check: open the link and compare with your answer.
translations.52c4bc8acddeaabfa7ade463: Track the agent with reports, a failure log, and triggers, and keep your judgment with you.
translations.e2e16d04c480aec3a934bdf3: A report is the summary the agent delivers at a scheduled time, saying what it did. A good report has a few simple numbers (how many sent, confirmed, pending), the list of cases it sent to you for decisions, and the list of errors. It fits on one screen and takes two minutes to read. The golden rule: error is never hidden—it always appears in its own section.
translations.7c7d5d82e80692938d3426c8: Without a report, you only find out what the agent did when something goes wrong and someone complains. With a report, you see the problem the same day. A report that only shows success is worse than none: it creates false confidence. It’s from this that you decide whether the agent moves up or down a level.
translations.b640a54ff030e630a5192833: Simple numbers: 3 to 5 counts you understand at a glance.
translations.285091ed26e13eaea93b313a: Cases sent to you: what needs human decision-making.
translations.7dbc2d88062a8507fc355cbd: Errors: always in their own section, even if it’s “none.”
translations.99ce74b3fcdd3f8fca018bd0: Fixed timing: every day or every week, always at the same time.
translations.d3d018a9f1ebb17706aacece: The failure log is a simple table where each agent error becomes a row: date, what broke, the smallest correction, and which line in the Agent Sheet was changed. A log—technical name for this kind of record—is just that: a dated note of what happened. It’s not an incident report or meeting minutes; it’s one line, written on the spot, with no narrative.
translations.79b8ce1ac166d95db22977e8: After about ten lines, the pattern appears on its own: the errors cluster around the same rule, the same source, or the same type of client. Without a log, each error looks new and you end up rewriting everything. With a log, you see that a single protection would have been enough—like a cap, an extra check, or an additional prohibition. It’s also the evidence to move the agent up or down a level.
translations.7e205677c2b2e050ffd69edc: Date: when the error was noticed.
translations.67332350296b88bf24a14c6a: What broke: the fact, in one sentence, with no blame.
translations.9d12b3aec833ec31b19a91e6: Smallest correction: the smallest change that prevents repetition.
translations.eff8ad9c0cfe28b33dc2ca58: Rule changed: which line of the Agent Sheet changed.
translations.7445a8fc8e18cb9d58c9f175: ⟪P0⟫3⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫Triggers: when it stops and calls you⟪P3⟫
translations.28d2761c2cbf3e4ca9b64304: Triggers are the situations where the agent stops what it’s doing and calls you immediately, without waiting for the report. This is escalation, also called escalade: handing the case to whoever has authority to decide. Good triggers are concrete and observable, such as “client threatening to complain,” “drop above 50%,” or “two patients at the same time.” Each Agent Sheet should have 3 to 5 triggers.
translations.456b350c2c6c6b4880971d38: The report shows what happened; the trigger prevents the worst from happening before the report. Without triggers, the agent tries to solve on its own situations that require judgment—and that’s where serious complaints are born. Working triggers are also the criterion for reaching N4: without tested alarms, the whole process can’t be in the agent’s hands.
translations.e890fb9530ee71f11117f95e: Concrete: something the agent can recognize without interpreting.
translations.ed7700cbbd9810e72470a6d9: Urgent: it can’t wait for end-of-day reporting.
translations.181683249cc48563951e65f0: Clear action: it stops, alerts you, and doesn’t try to resolve it.
translations.9ee92637c8defb046e2505ac: Tested: each trigger has been through a test before being turned on.
translations.9927ab8933d3143f3822fade: ⟪P0⟫4⟪P1⟫⟪P2⟫The ritual: 2 minutes per day, 10 per week, 1 review per month⟪P3⟫
translations.723bee10bc676fe22dbb30b0: Supervision isn’t just watching the agent work; it’s a short, fixed ritual. Every day: 2 minutes—read the report, handle the cases sent to you, and log errors in the failure log. Every week: 10 minutes—re-read the errors and adjust one single rule in the Agent Sheet. Every month: ask whether the level is still right and whether the task is still the same. Before turning it on, an extra step: the 3 tests passed, and the team knows there is an agent.
translations.306c6887656a8ca624656aae: Without a ritual, supervision happens only when something explodes—and by then it’s too late. With a ritual, the cost of supervision stays small and predictable, fitting into a business owner’s schedule. Adjusting one rule per week, not five, lets you know which change solved the problem.
translations.224e51a4b03c9427864a7fc3: Before turning it on: 3 tests, updated source, team informed.
translations.60458259510c3336d71c3d1e: Every day: 2 minutes in the report and in the cases sent to you.
translations.5ddb5db32aaafc340e858e44: Every week: 10 minutes and one rule adjusted.
translations.609d89ea97c2e8c699704f24: Every month: is the level still correct, and is the task still the same?
translations.db06fc48b3931fe283683c8b: The agent executes, analyzes, and even decides within the limits of the Agent Sheet—but the responsibility for the outcome remains yours. Supervision here is the management function: set objectives, establish limits, evaluate results, correct failures, decide exceptions, and evolve the process. Auditing—checking by sampling that the work is correct—is part of that. The agent expands your capacity; it doesn’t replace your judgment.
translations.643c61e973cb454891c88b39: When something goes wrong with a client, “it was the AI” isn’t an acceptable answer for anyone: not for the client, not for the law, and not for you. Knowing what can’t be delegated prevents handing the agent decisions that require human context—like an exception for an old client or a sensitive case with a student. Your role shifts from doing everything to deciding what matters.
translations.94215e606380b1d31eec9f52: Judgment: exceptions, new cases, and dilemmas stay with you.
translations.72cea0c5b81bb96d10cdf783: Auditing: check by sampling, even when the report is clean.
translations.974bf1d60c18352349169c12: Limits: only you move the level up or remove a prohibition.
translations.f3a4fe1eae47099390097edc: Responsibility: the outcome speaks in your name.
